meta.blurb: A rich Venetian fell ill at forty and chose to live simply. He wrote that he then enjoyed a long and happy old age. Discover his plain meals, calm habits and four short writings, and what we may still learn.
meta.bible: Luigi Cornaro (Alvise Cornaro in Italian): a nobleman of Venice who lived most of his life in Padua; the year of his birth is uncertain (later fifteenth century); he died in Padua in 1566, perhaps close to one hundred years old. His book: the Discourses on the Sober Life (Discorsi della vita sobria), four short parts written when he says he was about eighty-three, eighty-six, ninety-one and ninety-five; this retelling follows the four parts in order, then looks at his death, his fame and what modern science says. Venice: the city of canals where he was born. Padua: the Italian city where he lived and farmed. Italy: the country. Key facts from his own account: at about forty he was often ill and his doctors warned him; he began a strict, sober life with about twelve ounces of food and fourteen ounces of wine a day; he felt better within days and said he was free of illness within a year; at about seventy his friends persuaded him to eat a little more and he fell ill, then went back to his old measure; at seventy-eight a coach accident left him injured and he recovered quickly; at eighty-one he wrote a comedy; he worked on farmland and building; he loved his grandchildren. Key terms: Sober life, Moderation, Ounce, Bloodletting, Temperance. His claims are his own report and cannot be checked; his exact amounts are not advice for others. This book is general information and is not medical advice. Voice and tone: warm, respectful and clear, a historical retelling that says plainly when something is uncertain; no gore; no invented quotes.

B1B2: Luigi Cornaro lived in Italy about five hundred years ago. He wrote a small book about how to live a long and healthy life.
Cornaro came from a rich and well-known family of Venice. We do not know the year of his birth exactly, but it was in the later fifteenth century.
In the first part of his book, Cornaro says that as a young man he lived for pleasure. He feasted late at night and drank a lot of wine with his friends.
By the time he was about forty, Cornaro was often ill. He had stomach pain, a fever and a terrible thirst that would not go away.
His doctors warned him that he might not live much longer. They said that only a simple and sober way of life could save him.
At first he did not want to give up his favourite foods. In the end he decided to follow the advice, because he wanted to live.
Cornaro made a simple but very strict rule for himself. Each day he ate about twelve ounces of food and drank about fourteen ounces of wine.
His meals were plain, but they were not poor. He ate bread, soup, egg, some meat and some fish, together with a little wine.
Cornaro reports that he began to feel better within a few days. Within a year, he says, all his illnesses were gone.
Cornaro found that when he ate less, the plain food tasted better. He also felt light and clear in the mind after meals.
Cornaro argues that the body needs very little to stay strong. In his view, everything that we eat above that amount only does harm.
His most famous habit was to leave the table while he could still eat a little more. He believed that this habit kept him light and well.
Cornaro did not say that everybody should eat exactly like him. In his view, a young or strong person may need more than an older or weaker one.
Cornaro did not give up wine, which he enjoyed. He said that wine is a gift when it is taken in small amounts, and a danger when it is taken without limit.
Eating carefully was not enough for him, as Cornaro explains. He also tried to avoid anger, hatred and long sadness, because he believed that they harm the body.
Cornaro also took great care to protect himself from the weather. He tried to avoid extreme heat and cold, and he tried not to overwork his body.
When Cornaro was about seventy, his friends worried that so little food would weaken him as he grew older. They begged him to eat a little more, and he agreed.
Within about two weeks, Cornaro became sad and short-tempered, and then he fell ill with a fever. He realised that the extra food had been too much for him.
Cornaro returned to his old measure of food and wine. He soon recovered, and after that he never changed it again.
At seventy-eight, Cornaro's coach overturned, and the horses dragged it some distance along the road. He was badly hurt in the head and the body.
The doctors wanted to take blood from him and to give him strong medicine. Cornaro refused, because he believed that his body would heal itself.
Cornaro says that he recovered far sooner than anyone had thought possible. He took this as proof of the value of a simple life.
Many people feared old age as a time of pain and sadness. Cornaro said that it can be a happy time, if the body has been looked after well.
Cornaro writes that in his eighties he slept well, ate with pleasure and sang every day. He says that his voice was stronger than in his youth.
Cornaro was not idle in old age, and he always found useful things to do. He took part in projects to drain marshland and turn it into farms, and he planned houses and gardens.
At the age of eighty-one, Cornaro tells us, he wrote a comedy. He says that he was happy and in good humour while he wrote it.
Cornaro also writes with great joy about his family. He had grandchildren, and he was proud of their health and happiness.
Cornaro still enjoyed travel and new sights in old age. He visited Venice and the hills near Padua, where he met friends and enjoyed the views.
At about eighty-six, Cornaro wrote a second part, because he was still well and wished to help others. He addressed it to a learned friend, and he urged the young to begin early.
Cornaro thought that it was never too late to start, but it was much better to start early. A young person who forms good habits, he said, could enjoy health for a very long time.
For Cornaro, the sober life was not only about food. It meant moderation in everything, in eating, in drinking, in work, in sleep and in feelings.
Some people told Cornaro that his small meals made life dull and joyless. He replied that he enjoyed his life more than they did.
At about ninety-one, Cornaro wrote a third part of his book. He said that he was still in good health, and that he could still walk and ride a horse.
Cornaro says that his eyes and ears still worked well, and that his memory was sharp. He was pleased that his mind had not grown dull.
Cornaro did not fear death, which he knew would come one day. He hoped that his end would be gentle, without a long illness.
At about ninety-five, Cornaro wrote the fourth and last part of his book. It is short and friendly, and it seems to be written to anyone who will listen.
Cornaro advised his readers to eat in a measured way and to live calmly. He believed that anyone who tried it would soon see the benefit.
Cornaro advised that every person should notice which foods make them feel ill. Even if you love them, he said, you should eat less of them.
Cornaro cared a great deal about the place where he lived. He says that he kept his rooms warm in winter and cool in summer, with fresh air and a good bed.
Cornaro was not a sportsman, but he stayed active. He walked, rode and worked on his land, and he spent much of his time outdoors.
Cornaro enjoyed the company of friends and tried to stay on good terms with everyone. He believed that peace of mind was a help to a long life.
Cornaro believed that old age has its own rewards. A long life, he said, brings wisdom, a calm mind and freedom from the wild desires of youth.
Cornaro died in the city of Padua in the year 1566. Accounts say that he died peacefully in his chair, but we do not know his exact age.
Cornaro's book was printed many times and translated into several languages. People read it for centuries, and some still read it today.
In many experiments with small animals, eating less food has led to longer lives. In people the results are not so clear, and research is still going on.
Many of Cornaro's ideas agree quite well with the advice of modern doctors. He valued regular habits, activity, friends, purpose and a calm mind.
Cornaro's exact amounts of food are not right for everyone. Children, pregnant women, sick people and hard-working athletes all need different amounts.
Almost all we know about his health comes from his own words. His age at death is uncertain, and one man's story cannot prove a rule.
The heart of Cornaro's book is simple: take care of the body, keep a calm mind and enjoy the people and work you love. A long life is a gift, but a good life matters more.
This retelling is general information and is not medical advice. Please talk to a doctor before you change your diet, especially if you are ill, pregnant or taking medicine.
C1C2: Luigi Cornaro, a nobleman of Venice who spent most of his life in the Italian city of Padua, lived in the sixteenth century and became famous for a small book about growing old well. He called it a book about the sober life, and he wrote it in his eighties and nineties, when he was already far older than most people of his time. This retelling follows its four short parts in order, and it says plainly where his claims are uncertain.

Cornaro belonged to a wealthy and respected family of Venice, the city of canals and merchants, in a century of great art and trade. The exact year of his birth is uncertain, since different writers give different dates in the later fifteenth century, but all agree that he was already an old man when his book appeared. Because of this uncertainty, his famous age at death should be treated with some care.

In the first part of his book, Cornaro looks back honestly at his younger self, a man who lived for pleasure and thought little about tomorrow. He feasted late at night, ate whatever he liked in large quantities, and drank freely with his companions. Nothing in his early life, he admits, suggested that he would one day become a teacher of moderation.

By the time he was about forty, Cornaro tells us, his years of excess had caught up with him, and he suffered from stomach pains, fevers and a thirst that nothing could quench. Illness followed illness until he felt that his life was slipping away from him. Like many readers of his book, he learned the cost of a habit only when the bill arrived.

His doctors, according to his account, gave him a stern warning that he was unlikely to live for long if he did not change. The only hope, they said, was a plain and sober life in which he ate and drank much less than before. It was not welcome advice, for he loved the pleasures of the table, but he could see that the alternative was worse.

At first he resisted, as anyone might, because the old habits were comfortable and the new advice seemed severe. In the end he chose to obey, and he took the new rule so seriously that he kept to it, with a few exceptions, for the rest of his life. The decision turned out to be the true turning point of a very long life.

Cornaro made himself a strict rule for eating and drinking, and he measured it carefully by weight. Every day, he says, he took about twelve ounces of solid food and about fourteen ounces of wine, an ounce being a small weight of roughly thirty grams in modern terms. That is a small amount, and it should be remembered that it was his own choice, not a recommendation for every person.

His meals were plain but never miserable, for he ate bread, soup, egg, some kinds of meat and some kinds of fish, together with his measured cup of wine. He chose the foods that agreed with him and left aside those that disturbed his stomach, however much he had enjoyed them in the past. The lesson he draws is that a person's own experience is the best guide to what suits him.

He reports that he felt better within days of beginning the new life, and that in less than a year he was free of every illness that had troubled him. We cannot check his account against any medical record, of course, and we do not know exactly what was wrong with him. Nevertheless, it is the story upon which the whole structure of his book depends.

One surprise, Cornaro says, was that he found great pleasure in simple food once he ate only as much as he needed, because hunger made every plain dish taste better. He also noticed that he felt light and clear in the mind after meals, instead of heavy and sleepy. Moderation, in his experience, did not take pleasure away but moved it to a better place.

Cornaro argues that the body needs far less food than most people imagine, and that the extra we eat for pleasure is rarely free of cost. In his view it overloads the stomach, clouds the mind and slowly wears away the health that we hope to keep. Modern doctors would agree that regularly eating much more than we need can lead to health problems, though they would not all accept his exact figures.

His most famous habit was to leave the table while he could still have eaten a little more, which is a custom that many cultures have praised. He believed that it kept him light in body, quick in mind and free from the heaviness that follows a large meal. It is a simple idea, and it asks for nothing but a little self-control at the right moment.

Cornaro did not claim that everyone should eat precisely what he ate, and he admits that people differ in age, strength and work. A young or strongly built person, he allows, may reasonably need more than someone who is older or frail. Each reader, in his view, should therefore find the amount that keeps him light and well, rather than copying another person's rule.

Cornaro never gave up wine, and he even praised it as a friend to the old when taken in measure, though he warned that it turns on those who take too much. His daily cup was weighed as carefully as his food, and he considered the discipline part of its pleasure. Today we know that alcohol carries risks of its own, so his example should not be read as advice to drink.

Careful eating was only half of his plan, for Cornaro also tried to avoid the great troubles of the mind, such as anger, hatred and long sadness. He believed that they wear down the body as surely as bad food, and he worked at keeping a peaceful spirit. Modern studies do link long-lasting stress and anger to poorer health, which suggests that he was right to care about it.

He also paid attention to the weather and to his own limits, avoiding great heat, great cold and any effort that left him exhausted. In winter he sought warmth and sun, and in summer he sought shade and fresh air, as a sensible person still does. Such care was simple common sense, but he practised it faithfully for many decades, and he wrote that it served him well.

When Cornaro was about seventy, his friends grew anxious that so little food would weaken him in old age, and they begged him to eat and drink a little more. Out of affection for them, and perhaps out of a little doubt, he increased his daily measure by a small amount. It was a kindly experiment, but the result was not what anyone had hoped.

Within about two weeks, he says, he became low in spirits and quick to anger, and soon afterwards he fell ill with a fever. He realised at once that the extra food and wine had been too much for him, even though it seemed a trifling increase to his friends. His body had grown used to a certain measure, and it had made its protest known.

He went back immediately to his old measure, and in a short time, he says, he was well again. The experience convinced him that the rule suited his own body, and he never again allowed his friends to talk him out of it. Whether the extra food was really the cause of his illness, nobody can say for certain.

At seventy-eight, he tells us, his coach overturned on the road, and the frightened horses dragged it, and him, some distance before they could be stopped. He was carried home with serious injuries to his head and body, and the doctors who were called to him feared that he would not live for more than a few days. It was a terrible test of everything that he had said about the strength of a body kept in good order.

The doctors, following the custom of the age, wanted to bleed him and give him strong medicines, but Cornaro refused, trusting that a body in good order would mend itself. We should remember that bloodletting was a common treatment in his day and that modern medicine no longer uses it for injuries of this kind. His decision should not be taken as advice to refuse the care of a doctor today.

He says that he recovered far sooner than anyone had expected, and that his friends were astonished to see him on his feet again. He took this as proof that a careful life stores up strength for a day of trouble, much as a thrifty person saves money for hard times. We can admire his resilience, though it is wise to remember that one case is only one case.

In his time, as in ours, many people dreaded old age as a long decline into pain, weakness and loneliness. Cornaro insisted that it could instead be the happiest part of life, provided that the body had been treated with care in earlier years. His own cheerfulness is the main evidence he offers, and it is more persuasive than any argument.

In his eighties, Cornaro writes, he slept soundly, ate with real enjoyment, walked and rode without trouble, and even sang every day, his voice stronger than it had been in his youth. Such claims come from the man himself, and we must read them as the proud report of a happy old person rather than as a medical record. Yet the picture that they draw of his old age is a warm and attractive one.

Cornaro was far from idle in his later years, for he took an active interest in turning wet marshland into fertile fields, and he planned houses and gardens as well. He describes the pleasure of making poor land productive and of watching the work succeed, and the joy of useful work plainly shines through his pages. Purpose, in other words, was an important part of his own recipe for a long and contented life.

At the age of eighty-one, Cornaro tells us, he wrote a comedy, a lively play full of honest laughter, and he was delighted to find that his mind was as playful as ever. He offers it as evidence that the spirit of an old person can stay as cheerful as that of a young one. It reminds us that the sober life he recommended was never meant to be a sad one.

Few passages in the book are warmer than those in which Cornaro writes about his family, and especially about his grandchildren, whom he describes with obvious pride. He delights in their health and in their company, and he sees in them the future that his careful life has allowed him to enjoy. Long life, for him, was not a goal in itself but a way of staying near the people he loved.

Cornaro still enjoyed travelling in his old age, and he describes pleasant journeys to Venice, the city of his birth, and to the hills near his home in Padua. He took delight in the old streets and in the company of friends, and he noticed that the journeys no longer tired him. A person who could travel with pleasure at eighty, he implies, had every reason to feel fortunate.

Some years later, at about the age of eighty-six, Cornaro took up his pen again, writing a second part in the form of a letter to a learned friend. He was still well, he explained, and he wished to help others by saying more about the way of life that had served him so well. His strongest wish was that the young should begin early, before they had a chance to spoil their health.

Cornaro believed that it is never too late to begin, since he himself had begun at about forty, but he thought that it was far better to start while young. A person who forms good habits early, he said, collects the benefit for many more years and avoids a great deal of unnecessary suffering. Habit, which is so strong a force in a bad life, becomes just as strong in a good one.

By the sober life, Cornaro meant something wider than careful eating, for it covered every part of ordinary living, including work, rest, sleep and the passions of the heart. In each of these, the aim was to avoid both too much and too little, and to keep the body and mind in a steady balance. This ancient idea of the middle path is found in many traditions, and Cornaro made it practical.

Some of his critics said that a life of such small meals was no life at all, since pleasure at the table seemed to them one of the great joys of living. Cornaro replied that he took more pleasure in his days than they did in theirs, because he was well enough to enjoy them. The disagreement is an old one, and each reader must decide where the balance should fall.

At about ninety-one, Cornaro wrote a third part, and he reported with satisfaction that he was still in good health, walking, riding and travelling as he always had. He said that he could climb a hill or mount a horse without help, and that his friends were astonished at his condition. As always, these are his own words, and it is wise to remember that they are his own report.

He reports that his eyesight and hearing were as good as ever, that he could read without difficulty, and that his memory and judgment had not grown dim. Many of his neighbours, he adds, were frail and ill long before they reached his age, which made him all the more grateful for his own condition. He draws from this the cheerful conclusion that old age need not mean losing the senses.

Cornaro was not afraid to think about death, which he treated as a natural end that comes to every living person. He hoped that his own would be gentle and that it would come without a long and painful illness, as he thought it should for those who live carefully. It seems to him that a person who is at peace with life will also be at peace with its ending.

At about ninety-five, Cornaro wrote the fourth and last part of his book, in a tone that is shorter, simpler and gentler than that of the earlier parts. It reads like a final conversation with a reader who has stayed with him for many years, and it repeats the central message without fuss. The man who had once feasted all night now wished only to leave his readers with a calm and cheerful lesson.

His advice, repeated once more, was to eat and drink in measure, to keep a calm mind, to be active in useful work, and to begin without delay. He believed that anyone who tried this way of life would soon feel the benefit, and he was glad to offer himself as a living example. The simplicity of the advice is part of its strength, since a rule that is easy to remember is easier to follow.

Cornaro also taught that each person should observe which foods and drinks disagree with him, and then avoid them, even when they are favourites. The stomach, he argued, is the best judge of its own business, and a sensible person learns its language. This still sounds like good advice, as long as it is not used as an excuse to avoid foods that a doctor has told us to eat.

Cornaro paid attention to the comfort of his surroundings, and he says that he kept his rooms warm in winter and cool in summer, with fresh air and a good bed. He did not see these details as luxuries, but as part of the same careful attention that he paid to his food. A person who respects the body, he seems to say, should give it a pleasant place to rest.

Cornaro was no athlete, but he remained active well into old age, walking, riding and working about his land, and he spent much of his time in the open air. His kind of exercise was gentle and regular, and it fitted naturally into his day. Modern doctors would add that regular movement is one of the best gifts a person can give to an ageing body.

Cornaro valued good company and a quiet conscience, and he seems to have tried to stay on friendly terms with the people around him. He thought that peace of mind was as necessary to a long life as good food, and he took care not to let quarrels poison his days. Today, studies of ageing often find that close friendships and a sense of purpose are linked with better health in later life.

Cornaro believed that old age brings gifts that youth cannot give, among them wisdom, calm judgment and a release from the restless desires that trouble younger people. He enjoyed the freedom of being able to look back on a long life and to see it as a whole. This is perhaps the most attractive idea in the book, and it does not depend on any rule about food.

Cornaro died in Padua in 1566, and later accounts say that he passed away peacefully in his chair, without a long illness. His exact age cannot be known because the year of his birth is uncertain, but he was certainly very old, perhaps close to one hundred. If so, he lived far longer than most of his neighbours and contemporaries did in that age.

The book was printed again and again after his death, and it was translated into several languages, including English, so that readers far from Italy could learn from the old Venetian. For centuries it was often recommended to anyone who hoped to live a long and healthy life. Its popularity shows how deeply people have always wanted to understand the secret of ageing well.

Scientists have studied for many decades whether eating considerably less, while still getting enough nutrients, can lengthen life. In many experiments with small animals it has done so, but in people the results are less clear and the long-term effects are still being studied. Cornaro's story is therefore a fascinating example of one possibility, rather than a proof of anything.

Many of Cornaro's ideas are in line with what modern research suggests about healthy ageing, including regular habits, gentle activity, close friendships, a sense of purpose and a calm mind. He also warned against the habit of eating to excess, which is a common cause of ill health today. It is remarkable that a man in the sixteenth century saw so much so clearly.

It would be unwise to copy Cornaro's exact amounts of food and wine, because they were his own choice and they do not suit every person. Children, pregnant women, people who are ill or underweight, and those who work or train hard all have special needs that a single rule cannot meet. Eating far too little can be just as harmful to the body as eating far too much.

Almost everything we know about Cornaro's health comes from his own pen, and an author may be more cheerful about himself than an outside observer would be. His age at death is not certain, and one lucky old man cannot prove that his method will work for others. These cautions do not make the book less charming, but they do mean that it should be read as a story and not as a medical guide.

The heart of Cornaro's book is simple and enduring, which is to look after the body with moderation, to keep a calm mind, and to enjoy the work and the people that give life its meaning. He wanted a long life, but he wanted above all a good one, and the two, he believed, supported each other. Five centuries later, the old Venetian's central idea still deserves a quiet and thoughtful hearing from us.

This retelling is general information about a historical book, and it is not medical advice. Cornaro's methods were his own and they belong to the sixteenth century, so anyone who is thinking of changing their diet, especially if they are ill, pregnant, young or taking medicine, should talk to a doctor first. Enjoy the old man's wisdom as a story, and take your own health decisions with proper professional help.
